tr.td: 13 December 1943, within a wider operation that ran from about 4 to 14 December 1943
Kalavryta, a mountain town in Achaea, in the northern Peloponnese, Greece
Troops of the German Wehrmacht's 117th Jäger Division
Almost all the male residents of the town; counts range from 463 to 497 for the town itself
Town burned; no reparations paid to the families; the German commander died in Soviet captivity in 1954
Major-General Karl von Le Suire, who the memorial site says ordered the operation at the end of November 1943
The capture of German soldiers by partisans in October 1943; the prisoners were shot around 7 December
Sources give over 15, 12 to 80, 12 and over, 14 and over, and 16 to 65
693 to about 700 civilians according to different sources; more than a thousand by "independent as well as Greek sources" cited by Greek City Times
Between 24 and 28 villages and towns, plus monasteries, depending on the source
"Topos Thysias" (Site of the Victims), erected in 1967 on the hill above the town
Museum of the Kalavryta Holocaust, in the former school, opened 2005
Ceremony every 13 December; the church clock is stopped at 2:34 p.m.
FIPRESCI says very few of the officers responsible were ever brought to trial; the memorial site says the bereaved families have not received reparations from Germany

content.p: On the morning of 13 December 1943, soldiers of the German 117th Jäger Division gathered the people of Kalavryta, a small mountain town in the northern Peloponnese, and separated them. Women, children and the elderly were shut into the school. The men and boys were marched to a hill above the town. By afternoon the men had been machine-gunned and the town was burning. Thirteen men survived the shooting, injured, and the people locked in the school escaped the flames.

The killing at Kalavryta was one of the largest massacres of civilians carried out by Wehrmacht soldiers in the Second World War. It was also the climax of a ten-day sweep through the surrounding mountains that destroyed villages and monasteries and killed hundreds more people. The day is remembered through the stopped clock in the town's church, and the memorial site notes that the bereaved families have not received reparations from Germany.
content.h2: A reprisal policy and a hostage crisis
content.p: Italian forces had held the region since May 1941. The 117th Jäger Division came in during April 1943 as reinforcement, after the partisans grew more active. According to the memorial site, the unit had earlier served in Serbia as the 717th Infantry Division, where it had killed large numbers of civilians, among them the victims at Kraljevo in October 1941.

By the autumn of 1943 the German forces were openly threatening to kill 50 Greek hostages for every German soldier killed. The project Memories of the Occupation in Greece describes this "collective responsibility" as a defining feature of the occupation, and call the reprisal killings war crimes in direct violation of international law. They cite German calculations of about 30,000 Greeks "killed in action" between June 1943 and September 1944, civilians shot on account of real or imagined partisan activity, and a Greek government figure given at Nuremberg of roughly 91,000 Greeks murdered or shot as hostages.

The immediate trigger was a partisan ambush. An account by his son, preserved by the BBC, says that on 17 October 1943 communist ELAS partisans captured 81 men of the 749th regiment, part of the 117th Jäger Division, on a mountain track near the villages of Kerpini and Rogoi. The same account says four Germans were killed on the spot and three more, taken to hospital in Kalavryta, were later beaten to death. The memorial site gives a slightly different picture: partisans took about eighty soldiers hostage and demanded the release of 50 Greek hostages for each one. Greek City Times, by contrast, says that the partisan operation left some 80 German soldiers dead.

The prisoners were held at Mazeika, south of Kalavryta. According to the BBC account, the prisoners were held as prisoners of war until a decision was made to kill them as well. The memorial site says the partisans shot all their hostages at Mazeika on 7 December, as German troops closed in. Two prisoners survived the execution and raised the alarm.

The memorial site says that at the end of November the division's commander, Major-General Karl von Le Suire, ordered a military operation to free the soldiers and to carry out "retaliation measures" against the civilian population. The BBC account says over three thousand troops took part, advancing from Patras, Aigion and Tripolis, later from Corinth and Pyrgos, with Kalavryta as the objective. The first aim was to draw the partisans into battle and the second to find the prisoners.

When the Germans learned on 8 December that the prisoners had been killed, the BBC account says, Le Suire gave immediate orders for savage reprisals and flew to Kalavryta himself to instruct the newly appointed operation commander, Major Ebersberger, on how to carry them out. Greek City Times says the order was signed by Le Suire and told his men to "level" Kalavryta and the nearby village of Mazeika, along with other villages that had supported the partisans. It adds that the general witnessed the massacre personally. The memorial site adds that the Wehrmacht wrongly believed Kalavryta to be a centre of the partisan movement.

Several villages were hit first. The Municipal Museum of the Kalavritan Holocaust lists the men executed at each as part of the operation. On 8 December, Rogoi lost 66 men and boys and Kerpini 39, and 17 men were executed at Zachlorou. On the same day 25 monks and civilians were killed at the Mega Spilaio monastery. On 9 and 10 December smaller killings followed at Kerpini station, Souvardo and Vrachni, and Priolithos. The museum puts the dates of the whole operation at 5 to 14 December.

Greek City Times gives a detailed account of the morning. The townspeople were woken by church bells, and at about 9 a.m. the first soldiers appeared on the main road. Everyone was told to assemble at the school. Half an hour later the women and children were locked inside while the men were driven to Kappi Hill. The soldiers looted houses and loaded the spoils onto trucks while burning homes, churches and public buildings. The men, who could see their own houses burning, were ordered to dig their own graves before the signal for the shooting was given.

The BBC account, written by the British liaison officer's son, says the Germans had already set up concealed machine-gun posts, and that flares rising above the village were the signal. It says the men waited in the open ground believing they were to be deported. Survivors interviewed in a documentary reviewed by the film critics' federation FIPRESCI described being injured and then having to play dead among the bodies of friends and relatives as German officers went round finishing off the wounded with single shots. One man recalled that a bullet ricocheted off his scalp. Another said that he had been unable to open a gate to join his father at the execution.

Meanwhile the school was set alight. The memorial site says that those locked inside managed to escape the burning building. Greek City Times says the women then watched the rest of the town burn, and that the burial of the dead took them about 40 days. Because the departing troops had taken the food and burned nearby fields, they also faced starvation, the same article says.

The British officer, Captain Conal O'Donnell of SOE, a British wartime organisation, was in the area when the operation began. According to his son's account, he warned Greek friends in Kalavryta to take to the hills and then led a mule convoy of headquarters stores up Helmos, a mountain. His signals to Cairo, quoted in the account, said Kalavryta had been "occupied by Germans" and burned, and that guides forced to bury remains had been shot afterwards. When the Germans left, he returned to the town and was one of the first British officers there.
The figures differ by source and by what they count.

ul.li: The memorial site says 477 male residents of Kalavryta were killed, including boys under 15. A museum entry on the Google Arts and Culture project puts the town's dead at 465, with 13 survivors.
The BBC account says 497 men and boys were killed, and later in the same text says "at least 463".

For the whole operation, the Google Arts and Culture exhibit counts 696 civilians executed; keeptalkinggreece says 693, which it says are all named on memorials in Kalavryta and in other villages. Memories of the Occupation in Greece says a total of 700 men, including 22 women and children, died, with 24 villages and three monasteries destroyed.
Greek City Times says German reports claimed 696 inhabitants executed, while independent and Greek sources raise the total for Kalavryta and the surrounding area to more than a thousand.

content.p: The ages of the men taken also vary. The memorial site says all men above 15, Greek City Times men between 12 and 80, the BBC account all males aged 12 and over, FIPRESCI males aged 14 and over, and the Memories of the Occupation site men between 16 and 65. The number of places destroyed is given as 24 villages and towns, 28 townships and monasteries, or 28 communities, depending on the page. keeptalkinggreece adds that about 1,000 houses in Kalavryta itself were looted and burned and more than 2,000 livestock were seized.
content.h2: The myth of the merciful soldier
content.p: A story took hold after the war that one soldier, an Austrian, disobeyed orders and opened the doors of the burning school to let the women and children out. The BBC account calls this untrue and adds that the doors were not locked in the first place. Greek City Times reports that survivors' testimonies refute it. In 2021 the story caused a public dispute over a Greek feature film, "Eyewitness: Kalavryta 1943". Harilaos Ermeidis, president of the Association of Victims of the Kalavryta Holocaust and a former deputy mayor, said the scene in the trailer was a "provocative myth" refuted by all the eyewitnesses and officially by the town council. He said the association would sue the producers, a group that included the state broadcaster ERT. According to him, the film-makers had been told about the problem on a visit two and a half years earlier and had promised to leave the scene out.

Le Suire died in 1954 while a prisoner of war at Stalingrad, according to Greek City Times and FIPRESCI; FIPRESCI says he had been captured by Soviet troops about a year and a half after the massacre.

The World Socialist Web Site recounts that the 1947 to 1948 "Hostages Trial", one of the later Nuremberg proceedings, convicted eight of its twelve defendants, but that all were free by the early 1950s. It names Wilhelm Speidel, military governor of Greece from 1943, as responsible for directives authorising mass murders, including the Kalavryta massacre, and says he was released in 1951 from the Landsberg war criminals' prison. The World Socialist Web Site is a political outlet, and it argues that both the German and Greek authorities allowed the crimes to go unpunished.

FIPRESCI, reviewing the documentary "Kalavryta: People and Shadows", says that only token reparatory gestures have been made, that Germany's government has made no official apology, and that very few of the officers responsible were ever brought to trial. Separately, the German president Johannes Rau gave an address in Kalavryta. Speaking in German, he said the Wehrmacht had killed all the male inhabitants in revenge, among them children and young people, and spoke of deep sorrow and shame at the place. He invited a group of young people from Kalavryta to visit Germany.

In 1967 a memorial called "Topos Thysias", the Site of the Victims, was built at the place of the shootings on the hill. Four large marble plaques carry the names of the dead beside numerous graves, and a large cross is visible from far away. The memorial site says Kalavryta is seen as a symbol of Greek resistance since the War of Independence against the Ottoman Empire; the nearby Agia Lavra monastery, destroyed by the 117th Jäger Division in December 1943, is where the revolution began on 25 March 1821. The Municipal Museum entry says monks were killed at its entrance, five of them on 14 December.

A ceremony takes place every 13 December. The school became a museum in 2005. The church clock still shows 2:34 p.m.; the memorial site says that is when the massacre began, while the BBC account says it marks the time when the Germans destroyed the town.

Across the province, villages built their own monuments to the executed, the museum says, to preserve the memory of the executed civilians. The monument at Kleitoria, the last village destroyed in the operation on 14 December, commemorates 15 men executed and one who survived.
